tagline.text: A 24-hour fresh-flower market glowing through the night in Manila's Sampaloc

location.label: Location
location.text: Around Dos Castillas Street and Dimasalang Street, Sampaloc, Manila

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (early morning is best; All Saints' Day and Valentine's week are peak season)

children.text: Dangwa Flower Market is a fresh-flower market spread around Dos Castillas Street and Dimasalang Street in Manila's Sampaloc district. Flowers brought down from the northern Luzon highlands are traded here 24 hours a day, and you can buy a bouquet for far less than at an ordinary flower shop.

Dangwa Flower Market is a fresh-flower market in Sampaloc, Manila, centered on the crossroads of Dos Castillas Street and Dimasalang Street and stretching toward Lacson Avenue and Maria Clara Street. Locals sometimes call it Manila's "Bulaklakan," a place that sells flowers. The name "Dangwa" comes from the nearby Dangwa Tranco bus terminal. Since the late 1950s, buses from that terminal have carried flowers from Baguio and the Cordillera highlands to Manila, and the market grew up where those flowers were unloaded. English Wikipedia says the market began around 1976 in what was then a mostly middle-class residential area, and that it overtook rival markets in Quiapo and Baclaran during the 1980s and 1990s.

The market is not a single building but a string of small shops and street stalls along the road. Each shop has its own owner, and most sell both wholesale and retail. Mums, roses, orchids, gerberas, anthuriums, and asters are the main products, and the flowers come from farms across Luzon and Mindanao. Some varieties are imported from Thailand, the Netherlands, and Ecuador. Wikipedia reports that prices here are 50 to 90 percent lower than at ordinary flower shops in Metro Manila. Compared with what a mall florist charges for a bouquet, the difference is striking.

Dangwa is also famous for never closing. According to Wikipedia, one shop began operating around the clock in 1994 and others followed. Several guides still describe the market as open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Each shop sets its own hours, however, so some close at night. The busiest times are All Saints' and All Souls' Days (Undas) and Valentine's Day, and customers also flock here for graduation season, Holy Week, Mother's Day, and December.

For travelers, Dangwa is less a sight to tick off than a slice of everyday Manila life. Buckets and plastic wrapping pile up along the narrow street, and just watching bundles of roses and chrysanthemums change hands is a different kind of experience. If you spend a day in Manila, it fits well into a half-day route together with the University of Santo Tomas historic campus or Quiapo Church. It is also a practical shopping stop for Korean travelers and residents who need flowers as a gift.

blocks.title: A row of flower shops on Dos Castillas Street

children.text: The heart of the market is Dos Castillas Street, which runs between Laong Laan and Dimasalang Streets. Flower shops line both sides, so you can compare the prices and quality of many shops at once. The best approach is to walk the whole street first, look around, and only then buy.

Many of the flowers sold here come from farms in Baguio and the Cordillera highlands. Chrysanthemums, roses, carnations, and other flowers grown in the cool climate arrive in the early morning. If you go at dawn, you can see flowers that have only just been unloaded.

Along with mums, roses, orchids, gerberas, anthuriums, and asters, some items are brought in from Thailand, the Netherlands, and Ecuador. Imported roses and baby's breath look bigger and fuller than local ones, but they cost correspondingly more. Green foliage such as cypress, anahaw, and fishtail is sold alongside for filler.

blocks.title: Building your own bouquet stem by stem

children.text: You can pick flowers by the bundle or one stem at a time, so a bouquet can be built to fit your budget. You might pair three roses with baby's breath and greenery, or tie carnations tightly together. Plain kraft paper and a simple ribbon are enough to make it look lovely.

Besides fresh flowers, some shops sell dried flowers, bulbs, and local and imported plants. According to one profile, dried flowers go for around ₱15~35 each and last far longer than fresh ones. They are light and easy to carry home as souvenirs.

Several shops make custom arrangements and baskets of lilies, roses, carnations, and chrysanthemums for funerals. One local profile says some of these shops sit across from a hospital. Many people come to this market when they need flowers to pay respects to a Filipino acquaintance.

blocks.title: The spectacle around All Saints' Day

children.text: From late October to early November the market is at its busiest. The street fills with people buying flowers for the cemetery visit, prices rise, and local shops say demand can be several times the usual. It is worth seeing if you want to feel the energy, but be prepared for crowds.

blocks.title: The flower rush of Valentine's week

children.text: In mid-February, the price of a single rose rises to several times its usual level, and reports say the market stayed crowded until late at night with people buying bouquets. To buy in this period, either buy around February 12 in advance or go early in the morning before prices climb.

items.title: Dawn at the flower market
items.subtitle: When the fresh flowers come in

children.text: Arrive at Dos Castillas Street by taxi or Grab. In the early morning the flowers have just arrived, so there is more variety, and there is a little more room to bargain.
Walk the whole street once and compare the prices of roses, chrysanthemums, and carnations. The same flower is priced differently from shop to shop, so check two or three shops before buying.
Pick the flowers you like, buy them stem by stem, and have the shop wrap them. The simpler the wrapping, the cheaper it is.
Have breakfast nearby, walk through the market lanes once more, and then head to your next stop.
The early start has its own reward: the street is quiet and good for photos. If your schedule slips, remember that opening hours differ from shop to shop, so check on site.

items.title: Half-day route in north Manila
items.subtitle: From the flower market to the University of Santo Tomas and Quiapo Church

children.text: Look around Dangwa Flower Market and buy a bouquet as a gift if you need one.
Cross Lacson Avenue and tour the University of Santo Tomas historic campus.
Eat lunch at a nearby restaurant and then head toward the city center.
Visit Quiapo Church and the market streets around it.
From central Manila (Ermita or Malate), a taxi or Grab takes about
30 minutes to 1 hour
depending on traffic.
You can also transfer to a jeepney or taxi from LRT-1 Doroteo Jose Station or LRT-2 Legarda Station. Route-planning services describe a jeepney from Doroteo Jose toward Lacson Avenue that takes about
10 minutes
and costs
An older guide says to take the LRT-1 to Tayuman Station and ride a jeepney marked "España–Lardizabal." Routes may have changed, so check on site.
Public transit directions rely on older articles and automated route planners and may not be accurate. Check with an app or a local.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport to the city takes about
1 hour
by taxi or Grab, depending on traffic. It takes longer at times of heavy congestion.
The market is something you explore on foot. The stretch from Dos Castillas Street to Dimasalang Street is short, so a full loop does not take long.
When you take your flowers back to your lodging, a taxi or Grab is easiest. Hold the flowers on your lap so they are not crushed.

The best time of day is early morning, roughly between 5 a.m. and 8 a.m., when the flowers have just arrived. The selection is wide, the flowers are in good condition, and bargaining is a little easier. By daytime, sun and heat wilt the flowers quickly and the choice shrinks.

Across the year, a quiet weekday feels very different from peak days such as All Saints' Day or Valentine's Day. If you only want to watch, going on a peak day on purpose is fine, but if you want to buy cheaply, avoid the peaks.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: All Saints' Day and Valentine's week bring the biggest crowds and highest prices
Demand for graduations, Holy Week, and Mother's Day. Flowers wilt quickly in daytime heat
Rainy days make the street muddy and you need an umbrella. Preparation for All Saints' Day begins in late October

There are not many places to stay right around the market, so most visitors stay in other areas such as Ermita, Malate, or Makati and come in for the day. If you plan to go at dawn, line up a taxi or Grab in advance. If you stay in north Manila, lodging toward Quiapo and Santa Cruz is close by.

Food around the market is mostly street food, fast-food outlets, and small eateries in the nearby lanes. One guide places the market near a fast-food outlet on Laong Laan or Dimasalang Street. Early in the morning, a light bite of hot soup or bread is about right. Shop hours change, so check on site.
To buy cheaply, go between 5 and 8 a.m. and walk the whole street to compare prices before you buy.
If you choose flowers by the bundle or stem, you can build a bouquet to fit your budget, such as three roses with greenery.
Ask for simple wrapping. Kraft paper and one ribbon are enough and keep the price down.
For Valentine's Day and All Saints' Day, buy about two days ahead or go early in the morning. At midday on the day itself, stock is thin and prices are higher.
For funeral flowers or large orders, order at least two days ahead.
Prices differ from shop to shop and bargaining is possible, so compare several. Imported roses in particular vary a lot.
Most shops take cash (pesos), so bring plenty of small bills.
If you have a long ride after buying, ask the shop to wrap the stem ends in wet newspaper or plastic.
On peak days like All Saints' Day the lanes jam up and cars cannot get close, so get out on the main road and walk.
This is a crowded narrow-lane market, so watch for pickpockets and traffic, and expect it to be hard to move around, especially in All Saints' and Valentine's weeks.
Keep your phone and wallet in a front pocket or a bag worn in front of you, and stay aware of your surroundings while taking photos.
Flowers in photos may differ in size and condition from the real thing. For online orders the real flowers can look different, so choose in person.
On rainy days and at All Saints' Day peaks the lanes get muddy and traffic jams, so leave extra time.
Hours and prices differ from shop to shop, and the amounts here are rough figures from the sources. Check on site.
When going at dawn or late at night, do not wander alone into dark back lanes. Stick to the main road and arrange your ride home by Grab in advance.

blocks.title: University of Santo Tomas Historic Campus

children.text: A university campus founded in 1611, a short way from the market along Lacson Avenue. It takes about
5–10 minutes
by taxi.
A church famous for its Black Nazarene, about
15–25 minutes
from the flower market by taxi, depending on traffic.
A market district selling clothes and goods cheaply, which you can combine with the flower market for a tour of Manila's everyday market streets. It takes about
20–30 minutes
by taxi, depending on traffic.
Manila's old Chinese quarter, easy to pair with a food outing. It takes about
20–30 minutes
from the market by taxi, depending on traffic.
